subject: Schlisio et al. (2008)
object: Schlisio et al. (2008) identified inherited loss-of-function missense mutations in KIF1B-beta in neuroblastomas and pheochromocytomas, and an acquired loss-of-function mutation in a medulloblastoma. They argued that KIF1B-beta is a pathogenic target of the 1p36 deletions that are frequent in neural crest-derived tumors.

subject: Schlisio et al. (2008)
object: Using an unbiased shRNA screen, Schlisio et al. (2008) found that the kinesin KIF1B-beta acts downstream of the EglN3 prolyl hydroxylase. They showed that KIF1B-beta is both necessary and sufficient for neuronal apoptosis when nerve growth factor (NGF) becomes limiting. This is a developmental apoptotic pathway on which VHL, NF1, RET, SDHB and SDHD act.

subject: Schlisio et al. (2008)
object: Schlisio et al. (2008) noted that KIF1B-beta maps to chromosome 1p36.2, a region frequently deleted in neural crest-derived tumors, including neuroblastomas.

subject: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011)
object: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011) sequenced the exomes of 3 unrelated individuals with hereditary pheochromocytoma who did not have mutations in known susceptibility genes, and found mutations in the MAX gene. The tumors lacked MAX protein and showed loss of heterozygosity caused by uniparental disomy, which supported a role for MAX alterations in the disease.

subject: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011)
object: In a follow-up study of a selected series of 59 patients with pheochromocytoma, Comino-Méndez et al. (2011) found 5 additional MAX mutations.

subject: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011)
object: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011) suggested that MAX mutations were associated with malignant outcome in pheochromocytoma. They also suggested that loss of MAX function correlated with metastatic potential.

subject: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011)
object: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011) suggested that MAX mutations are preferentially transmitted through the father.

subject: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011)
object: Comino-Méndez et al. (2011) proposed that the MYC-MAX-MXD1 network is involved in the development and progression of neural crest cell tumors. They cited 2 lines of support: rat pheochromocytoma (PC12) cells lack functional MAX, and MYCN is amplified in neuroblastoma.

subject: Taïeb et al. (2018)
object: Taïeb et al. (2018) studied 6 consecutive patients with MAX-related pheochromocytoma using contrast-enhanced CT and 18F-FDOPA PET/CT. Four were imaged at initial diagnosis and 2 at follow-up. All but 1 patient developed bilateral pheochromocytomas during their lifetime, and the tumours were often multiple within the same gland. The two lesions missed on 18F-FDOPA PET/CT were smaller than 1 cm and corresponded to nodular adrenomedullary hyperplasia.

subject: Taïeb et al. (2018)
object: Taïeb et al. (2018) reported 5 different mutations in the MAX gene among their 6 patients with pheochromocytoma. In silico analyses predicted that these mutations disrupt the Max/Myc interaction and/or abolish binding to DNA.

subject: Taïeb et al. (2018)
object: Taïeb et al. (2018) found that 18F-FDOPA PET/CT detected more lesions than CT/MRI in MAX-related pheochromocytoma (per-lesion sensitivity 90.9% vs 52.4%). 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT detected fewer lesions than 18F-FDOPA in 1 of 3 patients. 18F-FDG PET/CT was only faintly positive in 2 of 4 patients and underestimated extra-adrenal lesions in 1 patient. The authors concluded that 18F-FDOPA PET/CT should be considered the first-line functional imaging modality for these patients.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) updated a previously reported family with predisposition to pheochromocytoma (PCC) across three generations. The female proband (III-1) developed neuroblastoma of the broad ligament at 17 months. At 22 years she developed a right PCC, a ganglioneuroma at the site of the original neuroblastoma and an ileal schwannoma, followed 6 years later by a left PCC with a mature ganglioneuroma. She later developed a leiomyosarcoma of the mesosigmoid with metastases, a hepatic carcinoma at age 42 and a uterine leiomyoma. Her paternal grandfather had bilateral PCC at age 70.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: In the family reported by Cardot Bauters et al. (2020), the proband's youngest brother (III-3) presented at age 31 with a cardiomyopathy complicated by Takotsubo syndrome, which led to the diagnosis of bilateral PCC. His urinary normetanephrines were raised to 8 times the upper limit, while total metanephrines were normal; the authors noted this pattern is reminiscent of MAX-related tumors. The paternal uncle (II-3) developed an 11-mm hypervascular right adrenal nodule at age 56 with strong [18F]-DOPA uptake, which the authors considered suggestive of PCC or an adrenomedullary nodule.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: In a family with PCC, Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) used a next-generation sequencing (NGS) endocrine tumor panel to identify a germline heterozygous MAX variant, c.145T>C (p.Ser49Pro), in the proband's brother (III-3), who had bilateral PCC and was negative for the familial KIF1B variant. The MAX variant was also carried by the proband, her grandfather (both with PCC), her father and her uncle. It was classified as a VUS under ACMG criteria. Both PCCs from III-3 showed loss of the wild-type MAX allele, and structural modeling predicted that the variant is likely deleterious.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) found no loss of heterozygosity (LOH) of the wild-type MAX allele in the 2 PCCs of the proband, and Sanger sequencing excluded a second somatic MAX mutation. The authors noted that a high proportion of normal tissue in the samples could not be ruled out as the reason LOH was not detected.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) proposed that genetic susceptibility to PCC/PGL in this family is linked to the MAX variant with incomplete penetrance. The father (II-2) carried the variant but developed no adrenal lesion, and his metanephrines remained normal.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) concluded that the heritability of PCC in this family, previously attributed to a germline KIF1B variant (c.4442G>A, p.Ser1481Asn), is linked to the MAX variant rather than to KIF1B. They suggested that the KIF1B variant may have contributed to the proband's neuroblastoma, and that her leiomyosarcoma, her hepatic carcinoma and her father's lung adenocarcinoma may be independent of both MAX and KIF1B.

subject: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020)
object: Whole exome sequencing (WES) of the proband found no pathogenic variants in other PCC/PGL genes or in 30 cancer-predisposition genes. Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) then identified maternally inherited VUS in TFAP2E (p.R363C) and TMEM214 (p.G263S). LOH of the wild-type allele was found for TFAP2E in the proband's uterine leiomyoma and for TMEM214 in her leiomyosarcoma metastases, and the authors suggested these variants may contribute to her non-neural crest tumors.

subject: Seabrook et al. (2021)
object: Seabrook et al. (2021) reported an Australian family (family A) in which multiple individuals had pheochromocytoma, including bilateral and metastatic disease, and 2 children, so far without pheochromocytoma, had neuroendocrine tumors: a paravertebral ganglioneuroma in one and an abdominal neuroblastoma in the other. One individual had acromegaly, and immunohistochemistry of that person's pheochromocytoma tissue was positive for growth hormone-releasing hormone. Another individual, whose pheochromocytomas had previously been resected, had pituitary enlargement and elevated IGF-1.

subject: Seabrook et al. (2021)
object: In all members of family A who had pheochromocytoma, and in both children with neuroendocrine tumors, Seabrook et al. (2021) identified a germline heterozygous MAX variant, c.200C>A (p.Ala67Asp). The pheochromocytoma tissue showed loss of heterozygosity. Immunohistochemistry showed loss of MAX staining in the pheochromocytomas and in the other neural crest tumors, and in vitro studies confirmed that the variant causes loss of function.

subject: Seabrook et al. (2021)
object: Seabrook et al. (2021) described the proband of a second Australian family (family B), who had bilateral and metastatic pheochromocytoma, a prolactin-producing pituitary tumor, adenomas in multiple parathyroid glands, chondrosarcoma, and multifocal pulmonary adenocarcinomas.

subject: Seabrook et al. (2021)
object: In the proband of family B, Seabrook et al. (2021) identified a truncating germline MAX variant, c.22G>T (p.Glu8*).

subject: Seabrook et al. (2021)
object: Seabrook et al. (2021) concluded that germline MAX mutations are associated with pheochromocytomas, ganglioneuromas, neuroblastomas, and pituitary neuroendocrine tumors, and possibly with parathyroid adenomas and with the nonendocrine tumors chondrosarcoma and lung adenocarcinoma. They suggested that MAX is a novel multiple endocrine neoplasia gene.

subject: Nosé et al. (2022)
object: In their overview of the fifth edition of the WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumors, Nosé et al. (2022) described MEN5 as one of the newly defined familial cancer syndromes, along with MAFA-related syndrome and MEN4.

subject: Sahakian et al. (2024)
object: In a review, Sahakian et al. (2024) noted that recently described families carrying a MAX mutation show a phenotypic spectrum that evokes multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN). MAX is known to predispose to pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma. The authors suggested that these families point to another syndrome, MEN5.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) concluded that MAX germline mutations may cause a new type of multiple endocrine neoplasia originating from the neural crest, which they suggested be called MEN5.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) described a Chinese man (family A) diagnosed at age 24 years with right pheochromocytoma after more than 2 years of hypertension (200/110 mm Hg), who at age 36 developed a 3.8-cm left adrenal pheochromocytoma with elevated plasma norepinephrine, giving metachronous bilateral pheochromocytoma. No pituitary abnormality or other neuroendocrine tumor was found.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: In the proband of family A with metachronous bilateral pheochromocytoma, Lian et al. (2024) identified a heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 4 of the MAX gene (c.223C>T, p.R75*; NM_002382.5) by targeted next-generation sequencing of 24 PPGL genes, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant was also carried by his unaffected 13-year-old son. It had a CADD score of 36, and 3D modeling predicted protein truncation.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) described a 34-year-old Chinese man (family B) with asymptomatic simultaneous bilateral adrenal masses (2.8 and 2.2 cm), normal blood pressure, and normal plasma catecholamines and metanephrines. Bilateral pheochromocytoma was confirmed after adrenal-sparing surgery. Pituitary, neck, and calcium, calcitonin, PTH, GH, and prolactin studies were normal.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: In the proband of family B with bilateral pheochromocytoma, Lian et al. (2024) identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation in exon 4 of MAX (c.242_243dupAC, p.Q82Tfs*89). His parents were not tested. 3D modeling predicted shortening of the C terminus.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) described a 64-year-old Chinese woman (family C) with occasional paroxysmal headache, elevated plasma norepinephrine, and a 1.9-cm right pheochromocytoma. She carried a novel heterozygous missense mutation in exon 5 of MAX (c.473A>C, p.E158A; CADD 25, REVEL 0.528), predicted to alter the loop domain. The variant was also found in a daughter and a sister, aged 43 and 59 years, who had no biochemical or adrenal CT abnormalities.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: In a literature review of 109 MAX germline mutation carriers from 87 families, Lian et al. (2024) found that 101 (92.7%) developed pheochromocytoma at a mean age of 32.8 years (range, 13-80), with a male-to-female ratio of 1.3:1. Of these, 59 (58.4%) were bilateral (47 simultaneous, 12 metachronous) and 19 (18.8%) were metastatic. Eleven (10.9%) also had thoracic or abdominal paraganglioma, and 1 had isolated head and neck paraganglioma. Catecholamines were elevated in 61 of 63 tested, mostly with a mixed noradrenergic/adrenergic pattern.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Among the 109 MAX mutation carriers, Lian et al. (2024) found that 9 (8.3%) had pituitary adenomas: growth hormone-secreting tumors in 3, prolactinomas in 4, and mixed adenomas in 1, presenting with acromegaly and/or prolactinoma symptoms. Eleven (10.1%) had other neuroendocrine tumors, including 4 with primary hyperparathyroidism (1 with multifocal parathyroid adenomas), neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma/ganglioneuroma, C-cell hyperplasia, and pancreatic NET. Seven (6.4%) had non-neuroendocrine tumors such as renal oncocytoma and renal cell carcinoma, and 3 carriers were asymptomatic.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) found 53 distinct MAX germline alterations involving all 5 exons among 87 families, mostly in exons 3 and 4. Nonsense mutations made up 47.7%. The most common mutations were p.R33* (c.97C>T; 21.1%), p.R75* (c.223C>T; 13.8%), and p.A67D (c.200C>A; 7.3%), which the authors suggested may reflect family and/or regional aggregation.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) found no significant difference in age at diagnosis, or in rates of pheochromocytoma, metastatic disease, paraganglioma, pituitary adenoma, or other tumors, between carriers of missense and non-missense MAX mutations. They suggested the genotype-phenotype correlation is not strong.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) noted that only 22 (25.3%) of 87 MAX mutation families had a family history of PPGL, and 8 (9.2%) showed a clear paternal family genetic background. They suggested that de novo MAX mutations may be common, estimating a de novo rate of 65.8%.

subject: Lian et al. (2024)
object: Lian et al. (2024) recommended that all MAX germline mutation carriers receive a comprehensive baseline assessment for neural crest-derived diseases, including PPGL, pituitary adenoma, hyperparathyroidism, and ganglioneuroma/neuroblastoma, with lifelong surveillance that accounts for the risk of bilateral and/or metastatic pheochromocytoma.

subject: Haider et al. (2025)
object: Haider et al. (2025) described a large kindred with MEN5 caused by a germline MAX variant. The male propositus developed pituitary gigantism from a mixed growth hormone-prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma, which was controlled after 2 surgeries, medical therapy, and radiotherapy. He later developed bilateral and recurrent pheochromocytomas. After his death, an extra-adrenal myelolipoma was found that was negative on MAX immunohistochemistry. The kindred had an extensive history of pheochromocytomas or uncontrolled hypertension. The authors reported this as the first case of pituitary gigantism associated with a MAX pathogenic variant and described myelolipoma as a new disease association in MEN5.

subject: Haider et al. (2025)
object: In the propositus and in multiple affected and unaffected relatives from an MEN5 kindred, Haider et al. (2025) identified a novel germline heterozygous variant in exon 4 of the MAX gene, c.228delG. The variant was predicted to cause a frameshift and a truncated protein (p.Asn78Thrfs*92). The extra-adrenal myelolipoma was negative on MAX immunohistochemistry.

subject: Haider et al. (2025)
object: Haider et al. (2025) described MEN5 as an emerging syndrome of endocrine and non-endocrine tumors caused by germline pathogenic variants or genomic rearrangements of the MAX gene. MAX variants are mainly associated with risk of pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma, but a growing number of tumors in other organs, including pituitary adenomas, have been linked to them.

subject: Charoenngam et al. (2026)
object: Charoenngam et al. (2026) described multiple endocrine neoplasia type 5 (MEN5) as a newly recognized entity caused by heterozygous inactivating germline mutations in the MAX gene.

subject: Charoenngam et al. (2026)
object: Charoenngam et al. (2026) performed a systematic review of 45 studies covering 127 patients with germline MAX mutations. The median age at first tumor diagnosis was 29 years, and 37.0% of patients were women. The most frequent tumors were pheochromocytoma (112 patients; median age at diagnosis 31 years), pituitary adenoma (11 patients; median age 33 years), and paraganglioma (10 patients; median age 43 years). Among the pheochromocytomas, 38.3% were unilateral and 27.6% were metastatic, and most secreted norepinephrine.

subject: Charoenngam et al. (2026)
object: Charoenngam et al. (2026) found evidence implicating MAX loss in the development of paraganglioma, pituitary adenoma, ganglioneuroma, neuroblastoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, renal oncocytoma, myelolipoma, and liver sarcoma. They considered the causal link between primary hyperparathyroidism and MAX loss to be uncertain.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: In a review, Maggacis et al. (2026) stated that inactivating variants of the MAX gene (chromosome 14q23.3), which encodes a 160-amino acid transcription factor, cause MEN5 syndrome. The syndrome was designated in 2021, after MAX variants had been associated with phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) since 2011. They listed PPGL and pituitary adenoma as cardinal features, and parathyroid adenomas and pancreatic NET as less common features.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) explained that inactivating MAX variants prevent normal activation of the MYC-MAX heterodimer. This leaves MYC function unregulated and drives cell proliferation, differentiation and angiogenesis. They noted that the increased MYC activity is thought to produce a more aggressive subtype of neural crest chromaffin cells.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) summarised a series of 109 patients from 87 families with MAX variants. Of these patients, 92.7% developed phaeochromocytoma, which was bilateral in 58.4% and metastatic in 18.8%; mean age at diagnosis was 32.8 years. Co-existing tumours included paraganglioma (10.9%), functioning pituitary adenoma (8.3%) and other neuroendocrine tumours (10.9%). The catecholamine phenotype was generally mixed noradrenaline and adrenaline secretion.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) stated that the exact prevalence of MEN5 is unknown, but that it is thought to account for 0.8 to 1.9% of PPGL.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) noted that both loss of MAX immunohistochemical staining and loss of heterozygosity have been found in MAX-related phaeochromocytoma. They suggested these tests may help when a causative MAX variant is suspected, for example with a germline MAX variant of uncertain significance.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) noted that there are no formal guidelines for MEN5 surveillance. An international consensus statement on childhood PPGL recommended the following for carriers of a pathogenic germline MAX variant: annual clinical assessment from age 10 years, plus annual plasma metanephrines and MRI from neck to pelvis every 2 to 3 years, starting at presentation or from age 15 years.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) cited a patient with the pathogenic MAX variant c.97C>T (p.Arg33*) who had bilateral asynchronous phaeochromocytoma and a pituitary adenoma co-secreting prolactin and growth hormone. The adenoma showed loss of MAX expression on immunohistochemistry, consistent with loss of heterozygosity in the tumour.

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) cited a reported case of pituitary gigantism in a patient carrying a novel MAX variant, c.228delG (p.Asn78Thrfs*92).

subject: Maggacis et al. (2026)
object: Maggacis et al. (2026) noted that pituitary adenomas associated with MAX variants tend to be functioning and are typically of PIT1 lineage, secreting growth hormone and/or prolactin. MAX-associated lactotroph adenomas tend to respond well to dopamine agonists, whereas somatotrophinomas tend to need multiple lines of therapy. The authors added that the broader phenotype of MAX variants has been hypothesised to include other neural crest-lineage diseases, such as ganglioneuroma, neuroblastoma, parathyroid adenoma, chondrosarcoma, myelolipoma and lung adenocarcinoma.

subject: MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA, TYPE V
object: Increased circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 concentration
